canonical_name: Philip K. Dick and the Bible
definition: Philip K. Dick's engagement with the Bible across his life: a familiar text before 1974, then, after the experiences of February and March 1974, the principal framework through which he interpreted them — read as a book of the future, a cipher, a living organism, and a source his own novels had unknowingly reproduced.
pkd_relevance: No text appears more often in the Exegesis or does more work there. Acts, Daniel, Revelation, Malachi, the Wisdom of Solomon, John and 1 Corinthians each supply a structural idea: the Empire, Elijah's return, Holy Wisdom, the Logos, impaired sight and agape.
in_the_fiction: Overtly in VALIS, The Divine Invasion, The Transmigration of Timothy Archer and Deus Irae; by Dick's later account covertly in Flow My Tears (Acts), Ubik (the Logos) and A Scanner Darkly (1 Corinthians 13).
in_the_exegesis: From 1975 to 1981: the Bible as a book of the future, as code, as living information, and as the record of which God he had met.
intellectual_background: The Septuagint and its apocrypha; Philo's allegorical Torah; the Dead Sea Scrolls and Nag Hammadi codices; the Jehovah's Witnesses' apocalyptic reading of Daniel; modern esoteric readings such as The Decoded New Testament.
scholarly_debate: Whether Dick knew Acts before 1974; how far 1 Corinthians 13 structures the fiction; the open versus the frozen scripture of The Divine Invasion.
chronology_summary: Junior high: the Elijah radio serial. 1962–73: Corinthians, King James, rhymed couplets, the Scanner Darkly title, comparing translations. 1975: Acts and Flow My Tears; the Bible as a book of the future; the Wisdom of Solomon. 1976: the Bible as code. 1978–80: living scripture. 1981: YHWH; the Jerusalem Bible.
contradictions_summary: Seven, kept rather than resolved: his prior knowledge of the Bible; whether he had read Acts; the Bible dispensable or alive; code or incomplete code; which God; Bishop Archer as Christ figure or lawyer; one Jason or two.
editorial_notes: Every card was chosen and summarised by reading the passage. Machine-extracted claims about the Bible in the database are unreviewed and not used. Fiction passages are characters speaking (lane A); the Exegesis is lane B; scholarship lane C; biography lane D; letters and interviews lane E.
open_questions: Which Bible did Dick own before 1974? — raised under Before 1974. Letters show the King James, the New World Translation and the New English Bible by 1973, but no inventory of his books survives in this archive. Resolvable by: an inventory of his library.

Did Dick know Acts before 1974? — raised under 1975. He allows a forgotten reading; Butler denies any reading. Resolvable by: pre-1974 letters outside the Selected Letters, or annotations in his own Bible.

Was the Wisdom of Solomon letter of September 1975 sent to more than one person? — the same text is recorded once in the Exegesis ("Dear Doris") and once in the Selected Letters ("Dear Sherri"). Resolvable by: the original manuscripts.

What is Dick's source for Philo's living Torah? — raised under Living scripture. He copies a passage in quotation marks without naming the book. Resolvable by: identifying the quotation, likely an encyclopedia article on Kabbalah or Philo.
Which Exegesis passages in section 016 belong to 1978, and which to 1980? — raised under the cautions. Resolvable by: matching each segment to the folders of the published edition.
The Book of Acts is traditionally ascribed to Luke; Dick calls it "Paul's". Slip, or a reading? — raised under 1975. Unresolved.

dossier_sections.heading: Philip K. Dick and the Bible
body: The Bible is the text Philip K. Dick argued with longest. He knew it before he believed anything about it: he dates his first reading to a junior-high radio serial about Elijah {{PKB-INT-ELIJAH}}, took the title of A Scanner Darkly from Paul in 1973 {{PKB-LET-1973B}}, and was comparing translations of Ecclesiastes and 1 Corinthians five months before the experiences of February and March 1974 {{PKB-LET-1973C}}. After 2-3-74 it became the main instrument with which he tried to understand what had happened to him.

What makes his use of it distinctive is not piety but method. He read scripture as a description of the present ("The Bible is a book of the future" {{PKB-LET-1975-CLAUDIA}}), as a cipher ("The Bible is code" {{PKB-EX-1976-ACTSPRISON}}), as a living organism — the esoteric Torah of Philo, the plasmate {{PKB-EX-1978-TORAH}} — and as a source his own novels had tapped without his knowing: Flow My Tears, he came to believe, reproduces the Acts of the Apostles {{PKB-ESS-RASCH}}. Each of these readings is held alongside the others, and several contradict each other. This page keeps them apart.

The page is organised in two ways at once. The essay below runs roughly in order, from before 1974 to 1981. The index of books and themes underneath lets you go the other way: pick Acts, Daniel, Malachi or 1 Corinthians and see every passage in the archive that turns on it, whatever its date or source. Every bracketed reference in the essay opens the card it cites.

dossier_sections.heading: Before 1974: a reader, not yet a believer
body: Dick's own account starts in junior high school, with The Light of the World, a daytime radio dramatisation of the Bible. He came in during the Elijah episodes, went and read the story, and wanted above all to hear the voice Elijah hears on Mount Horeb {{PKB-INT-ELIJAH}}. A schoolfriend remembered the same years differently — an atheist who could not prove God existed and who also tried to start a Bible Club {{PKB-SCH-SUTIN-02}}. The two accounts agree on the date.

The letters of the 1960s and early 1970s show a writer for whom the Bible is common property. In 1962 he describes coming out of years of agoraphobic misperception in Paul's words: he "did see face to face" {{PKB-LET-1962}}. In 1964 the King James Bible is his example of a grand style that cannot make imitation serious {{PKB-LET-1964}}. In 1972–73 a dream about setting the Bible into rhymed couplets becomes a running joke with friends {{PKB-LET-1972}} {{PKB-LET-1973A}}.

Two documents from 1973 show more than familiarity. In March he explains to Carol Carr that the title of the novel he is writing, A Scanner Darkly, is a pun on 1 Corinthians 13:12 {{PKB-LET-1973B}}. In September he sets three translations of 1 Corinthians 15:51 side by side for his agent and prefers the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation as "so direct, so—honest" {{PKB-LET-1973C}}. Ubik, written years earlier, already ends its chapter epigraphs with a product that speaks as the Word of John's Gospel {{PKB-FIC-UBIK}}.

This matters because Dick later said the opposite. In 1976 he told his mother that when he saw the Iron Empire in 1974 "I was almost totally unfamiliar with the Bible" {{PKB-LET-1976-HUDNER}}. The claim makes his visions independent of his reading; his own letters do not support it, at least for the Bible as a whole. The contradiction is recorded below rather than resolved.

dossier_sections.heading: 1975: Acts and Flow My Tears
body: The discovery that organised the rest arrived in 1975. Dick's earliest dated statement of it in this archive is a July letter to Göran Bengtson: Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said "on close inspection, contains a number of passages evidently derived from or which refer to the" Book of Acts, which he connects to a theory that his unconscious is an Attic Greek {{PKB-LET-1975-BENGTSON}}. To Claudia Bush he reads the novel's closing embrace between Felix Buckman and a black stranger as the Feast of Agape, and does not know how it got in {{PKB-LET-CLAUDIA-AGAPE}}.

The public telling came in the 1978 speech How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later. His Episcopalian priest, hearing the gas-station scene described, recognised it as Philip meeting the Ethiopian in Acts 8 {{PKB-ESS-RASCH}}. Dick then found Felix, the Roman official who interrogates Paul, and a single Jason sheltering a fugitive — an inversion of his own Jason Taverner {{PKB-ESS-JASON}}. In the Exegesis the name Felix becomes a key: it "points to the Biblical nature of the dream" {{PKB-EX-1975-FELIX}}.

Over the following years the Acts parallel grows from coincidence into doctrine. Acts is "a police state" and "how it really is" {{PKB-EX-1976-ACTSPRISON}}; the canonical Acts "leaves out crucial information" that survives only in the novel {{PKB-EX-1976-OMITS}}; the recipient of the revelation lives in reality "as interpreted through + by the Acts lens/grid", a contemporary of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-CONTEMPORARY}}. Dick himself allows that he may simply have read Acts and forgotten it {{PKB-EX-1978-UNCONSCIOUS}}.

dossier_sections.heading: A book of the future: Daniel, Revelation and the Empire
body: On 27 February 1975 Dick wrote the sentence that governs his apocalyptic reading: "The Bible is a book of the future." The New Testament and the Old Testament oracles are "about tomorrow"; the backdrop is familiar, the events new {{PKB-LET-1975-CLAUDIA}}. Daniel and Revelation, "the two apocalyptic books", become the lens for the tyranny he believed he had seen thrown down in 1974.

The identifications are explicit and they move. Revelation's beast is Rome, and its fall is the Parousia {{PKB-EX-1975-REVROME}}. With the Jehovah's Witnesses he reads Daniel's statue with feet of clay as the Anglo-American Empire {{PKB-EX-1975-CLAYFEET}}. By 1976 the scene is Cyrus's siege of Babylon, with Daniel the prisoner, and the equation runs Babylon = Rome = Washington DC = Moscow {{PKB-EX-1976-BABYLON}}. Apocalyptic vision, he argues, is a glimpse of eternal reality behind time, true "in Daniel's time, in John's and mine" {{PKB-EX-1975-APOC}}.

He knew how this looked. In the same 1976 sitting he copies a sociological observation from the Britannica — only the alienated yearn for divine intervention — and adds: "I fit this latter class" {{PKB-EX-1976-ALIENATED}}. In VALIS the hunt for Nixon in Daniel is given to the cynic Kevin, to Fat's amusement {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-DANIEL}}. And in October 1981, during a lightning storm, he read Revelation and Daniel to his frightened cats {{PKB-LET-1981-CATS}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Elijah, Malachi and the returning Spirit
body: Malachi's last chapter promises that Elijah will be sent before the great and terrible day of the Lord. Dick used it more than any other prophetic text to name what possessed him. The Lord of Hosts suddenly coming to his temple is how he describes seeing the world as a living organism {{PKB-EX-1975-MALACHI}}; the Spirit of Elijah that Malachi promises is, he decides, "the Old Testament Hebrew concept for the Christian Holy Spirit" {{PKB-EX-1975-ELIJAH}}. In 1976 he quotes the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings — and reminds himself what Elijah did to Ahab {{PKB-EX-1976-SUN}}.

The same verse appears in VALIS, where its promise of healing sharpens Fat's despair over his dying friend {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-MALACHI}}, and Elijah walks into The Divine Invasion as Elias Tate. In August 1981 the figure Dick reaches for is still the one from the radio serial: God as the "still small voice" that spoke to Elijah {{PKB-LET-1981-STILLSMALL}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Holy Wisdom from an apocryphal book
body: Dick's St. Sophia — Holy Wisdom, Hagia Sophia, the figure who becomes Zina in The Divine Invasion — came to him through a book many Protestants do not count as scripture. In September 1975 he explains to a friend that his church now recommends the apocrypha, and that the Wisdom of Solomon, part of the Septuagint the early Christians used, "was as sacred as any book of the Hebrew Scriptures" {{PKB-EX-1975-SEPTUAGINT}}.

From it he builds a theology of the Incarnation: Sophia, the world-builder of the wisdom books, entered human form and lost some of her powers while she was here {{PKB-EX-1975-WISDOM}}. By 1977 he identifies the voice in his head with "the Logos, or St. Sophia, Holy Wisdom" {{PKB-LET-1977-JAYNES}}; in 1981 Wisdom speaks in the novel as the living Torah, the blueprint of the universe {{PKB-FIC-DI-TORAH}}.

dossier_sections.heading: The Bible is code
body: The idea that scripture is a cipher appears first in fiction. In March 1975 Dick outlines a novel in which a man possessed by a Qumran Essene finds "the New Testament is in cypher" {{PKB-LET-1975-ORNSTEIN}}. By 1976 he states it about the world: the Bible "isn't about the past; it's code to describe our world", and Acts is now {{PKB-EX-1976-CODE}}. To decode it is to read the New Testament as "an encoded instruction manual by which to become part of Valis" {{PKB-EX-1976-MANUAL}}.

The cipher has a structure. In one entry the testaments are opposing players: "O.T. encodes + N.T. decyphers", dark against light {{PKB-EX-1978-DECYPHER}}. And it is incomplete. The same Exegesis that calls the Bible code insists that Acts as canonised leaves out what Flow My Tears preserves {{PKB-EX-1976-OMITS}}. By 1981 Dick reads his own novels as two ciphers in opposite directions: Flow My Tears political on the surface with a hidden stream from Acts and Daniel, VALIS theological on the surface with a hidden political one {{PKB-LET-1981-REVERSE}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Living scripture
body: Early in 1975 Dick thought the Bible was dispensable: suppress it entirely and the experience it records would "spring to life within given human minds once more" {{PKB-LET-1975-WILLIAMS}}. He ended in the opposite place. Copying out Philo's image of the Torah as a living being, body the literal text and soul the hidden meaning, he exclaims: "This is the Acts material, the living information I saw" {{PKB-EX-1978-TORAH}}.

The carriers of this living text are manuscripts that came out of the ground. Thomas, the personality he believed took him over, slumbered "perhaps in a jar at Qumran" {{PKB-EX-1976-QUMRAN}}; the huge open books he saw were the Qumran scrolls Bishop Pike saw, passed to him as plasmate {{PKB-EX-1978-SCROLLS}}; the Nag Hammadi codices may be "the actual Secret Living" blood of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-NAGHAMMADI}}. The Logos of John's prologue is the bridge between text and organism, and Ubik's "I am the word" is the proof he finds in his own fiction {{PKB-EX-1978-UBIKWORD}}.

The novels build the idea as objects. Elias's holographic Bible in The Divine Invasion yields different messages at every angle, "an infinitude of knowledge that ceaselessly changed" {{PKB-FIC-DI-HOLOGRAM}}; Zina declares "I am the Torah" {{PKB-FIC-DI-TORAH}}. Tseng reads the open, living scripture against the novel's Church, which wants to freeze it {{PKB-SCH-TSENG}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Which Bible: translations and editions
body: Dick did not read one Bible. The archive shows him using at least five, and paying attention to their differences: the King James, whose cadence he took for granted {{PKB-LET-1964}} and a copy of which he gave his mother {{PKB-EX-1978-KJV}}; the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation, which he preferred in 1973 {{PKB-LET-1973C}} and whose reading of Daniel he borrowed {{PKB-EX-1975-CLAYFEET}} while rejecting its theology of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-MATTHEW}}; the New English Bible, which he quotes for John 10 {{PKB-LET-1975-KORMAN}} and checks for the word "secret" in 1 Corinthians 2 {{PKB-EX-1981-SECRET}}; the Jerusalem Bible, "an official Catholic Bible", whose notes he studies in 1981 {{PKB-LET-1981-BLOODWATER}} {{PKB-LET-1981-AGAPE}}; and Jerome's Vulgate, the source of the word he wanted on his gravestone, Dilexi {{PKB-LET-DILEXI}}.

He also read through intermediaries: the Septuagint's apocrypha {{PKB-EX-1975-SEPTUAGINT}}, The Decoded New Testament's esoteric glosses on the Crucifixion {{PKB-EX-1975-DECODED}}, and reference books on Exodus when a television drama got Passover wrong {{PKB-LET-1975-CBS}}. The last novel's bibliography cites the Jerusalem Bible, and its narrator notices the change of translation in a bishop's hands {{PKB-FIC-ARCHER-DIM}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Which God?
body: Dick never decided which God of the Bible he had met, and his answers are incompatible. In 1977 he tells Julian Jaynes it was "not so much the creator god of our Bible" as Plato's arranger {{PKB-LET-1977-JAYNES}}. Reading the Nag Hammadi codices, he concludes that Palmer Eldritch, explicitly the Christian God of that novel, is the Gnostics' blind demiurge {{PKB-EX-1978-YALTABAOTH}}. Late in 1980 it is the Cosmic Christ of John, distinct from the human Jesus, and its nature is agape {{PKB-EX-1980-COSMICCHRIST}}.

In April 1981 he reverses that: the king on horseback in the Tears dream is YHWH, judge and destroyer, "not the God of the N.T., the Xtian God of agape" but the God whom Moses knew, and VALIS is "a fusion of Exodus & Daniel" {{PKB-EX-1981-YHWH}}. Two years earlier the same figure was the young king, Christ as judge, of Daniel and Revelation {{PKB-EX-1978-YOUNGKING}}. The last novel gives the question to scholarship: the mysterious word in the Zadokite scrolls is anokhi, God's "I" in Exodus 20 {{PKB-FIC-ARCHER-ANOKHI}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Scripture in the novels
body: The fiction uses the Bible in two ways, and the difference matters. Overtly, characters quote and argue: Pete in Deus Irae calls the Bible "a chronicle of God's search for man" {{PKB-FIC-DEUSIRAE}}; Fat's journal is an exegesis because it treats his revelations as scripture {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-EXEGESIS}}; Bob Arctor understands the "glass darkly" verse and cannot be helped by it {{PKB-FIC-SCANNER}}. These are characters speaking, not Dick.

Covertly, on Dick's own later account, the novels carried scripture he did not know he had put there — Acts in Flow My Tears, the Logos in Ubik. That is a claim about the novels made from outside them, and the page keeps it in Dick's lane, not the fiction's. He could also turn on his own scripture-quoting characters: rereading The Transmigration of Timothy Archer, he decided its bishop uses the Bible "not as a man of God but as a lawyer" {{PKB-LET-1981-ARCHER}}.

dossier_sections.heading: What scholars say
body: Sutin places the Bible and the Dead Sea Scrolls in a lifelong, "virtually limitless" range of reading {{PKB-SCH-SUTIN-01}}. Butler makes 1 Corinthians a standing heading in his survey of every novel {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-02}}, traces Felix and Jason to Acts 17 {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-03}}, and states that Dick had not previously read Acts {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-01}}. An essay in Theory, Culture & Society reads the "glass, darkly" verse and its sequel, caritas, as the two halves of Dick's late thought {{PKB-SCH-TCS-01}}, and points to work comparing Paul's conversion in Acts 9 with February 1974 {{PKB-SCH-TCS-02}}. Tseng and the Extrapolation essay read The Divine Invasion's open Bible and its Job-like wager {{PKB-SCH-TSENG}} {{PKB-SCH-EXTRAP}}.

dossier_sections.heading: What this page does not claim
body: It does not claim that Dick's scriptural readings are correct, or that the coincidences he found in Flow My Tears are more than coincidences. It reports what he wrote and what others have written, in separate lanes: the fiction is characters speaking, the Exegesis and letters are Dick, the scholarship is scholars.

Dates are given per passage with the evidence for them. Exegesis section 016 carries a container date of October 1978 that its own passages contradict; passages from it are dated 1978–80 unless a stamp or folder places them more precisely. The 348 machine-extracted "claims" about the Bible in our database are unreviewed and are not used here; every card on this page was chosen and summarised by reading the passage, and every quotation is checked verbatim against its source before the page is built.

mention_cards.citation: Interview with Gregg Rickman, in Philip K. Dick: The Last Interview and Other Conversations
mention_cards.context: Asked by Gregg Rickman where his religious preoccupations come from, Dick goes back to junior high school and a daytime radio serial, The Light of the World, that dramatised the Bible. He tuned in during the Elijah episodes, then read the story for himself, and wanted above everything to hear the low murmuring voice Elijah hears on Mount Horeb. He says he heard such a voice two or three years later, during an eleventh-grade physics exam — and then, half-mocking, files the whole account as an enormous fantasy. It is the earliest date he ever gives for reading scripture, and it ties the Bible to the voice, not to doctrine.
mention_cards.pith: And I started reading the Bible and I read that part about Elijah.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick's own retrospective account, given in the last year of his life. Sutin independently records a Bible Club he tried to found in junior high (PKB-SCH-SUTIN-02).
mention_cards.passage: … When I was a kid—here’s your psychological theory. I will give you all the ammunition you need here for your “reductive psychological”— **RICKMAN :** It’s a theory. I didn’t say I believed it. [ _Laughter_ ] **DICK :** When I was in junior high school there was a soap opera on daytime radio called _The Light of the World_ , a story of the Bible. They dramatized part of the Bible. I happened to start listening during the part about Elijah. And I started reading the Bible and I read that part about Elijah. And it was my greatest wish in the world of anything to hear that low murmuring voice that Elijah heard. The voice of the Lord and that is the etiology of that psychologically. That junior high school kid within a few years—like would you believe two to three— got his wish and heard it during his final physics test in eleventh grade. Heard that voice but did not know that there was a connection there. So this is all an incredible fantasy on my part. It is one of the most organized, …

mention_cards.context: A long autobiographical letter about agoraphobia. Dick describes the world of the street as one he had experienced as hostile and aimed at him, and a stimulant that briefly let a stronger, more organised view of the world win out. He reaches for Paul to say what happened: he saw face to face, and never fully recovered the delusional view he had lived inside. Twelve years before 2-3-74 the Corinthians verse already names, for him, the moment a false world gives way.
mention_cards.pith: I did see face to face—and after that, never quite got back the delusional view
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … For instance, I had often stood by the hour at the front window of my house, gazing out... why? I did not know; I was only aware that I enjoyed—or rathei; wanted to—watch the street. Ah, existential psychiatry: its word, here: Mitwelt. The world-of-the-street, world with people. How did I experience that Mitwelt? As hostile, as directed against me. And, the stimulant drug encouraged a more pow­ erful impulse toward Worldview organization mometarily to triumph: as in the phrase, “We see as through a glass darkly, now face to face,” I did see face to face—and after that, never quite got back the delusional view which had grown up over most of my life. With the car, I began driving first around town, then out into the coun­ try, and, at last, as far as Missouri, Arkansas, Idaho, etc. The first restaurant I entered and ate …

mention_cards.context: Part of a long argument with James Blish about what makes a novel serious. Dick's answer is novelty: a serious book must be new, not formula, and the King James Bible appears only as the gold standard of borrowed grandeur that cannot by itself make imitation serious. A literary, not a religious, use — and a sign of how available the King James cadence was to him.
mention_cards.pith: There is no such thing as a “serious” novel which repeats what has gone before
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … for us all. So—back to the topic of the “serious” work of art. Surely that story was—is. We agree? Right. Okay. Now, to brass tack, to the Ursatz. (one) Serious does not mean not-funny (v. parts of _Ulysses,_ a lot of Beckett (such as WATT ALL THAT FALL, GODOT). In fact vide TOM JONES, both as book and as movie (grossartig Theater, das). But it does mean _new._ There is no such thing as a “serious” novel which repeats what has gone before, even if it apes the King James Bible and the Iliad put together. Maybe we want the word _original_ instead. Hence pop art can at least make the claim of being “serious” in that sense, just as Bauhaus art was, or dada. The bipolari­ ties are original-versus-formula, either your own formula or someone else’s. (two) Serious …

mention_cards.context: A comic dream reported to his French friend: Dick on stage accepting an award, Harlan Ellison alone in the audience laughing, and the award turning out to be for setting the Bible into rhymed couplets. He improvises a Genesis couplet and sets it against Luther's German, which he says he always liked. Fifteen months before 2-3-74, scripture is a joke he expects a correspondent to get.
mention_cards.pith: I had set the Bible into rhymed couplets.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Meanwhile, we are happy for you and Judy. Maybe he will inherit his father’s writing ability. Speaking of writing ability—I dreamed the other night that I was up on a stage making a speech of acceptance for an award, but I was not too clear in my mind what the award was for. Harlan Ellison was the only person in the audi­ ence and he was laughing. I finally was told what the award was for: I had set the Bible into rhymed couplets. I got out of there fast. mention_cards.citation: Letter to Art Spiegelman and Michele Gross, January 7, 1973
mention_cards.context: Written from Fullerton during the chaotic early months of 1973. The rhymed Bible from the Duvic dream has become a running gag: Dick reports the project coming along fine, one couplet finished after four months' work, undertaken at the dream's bidding for the glory of God and for profit. The joke matters because it is a joke: the Bible is there to be played with.
mention_cards.pith: for the Glory of God, as well as for fun and profit in my spare time.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Despite the confusion I think I can safely say that we’re getting nowhere, and that in some respects is a relief. Mary is still alive, I am, Tessa pretends to be, the enemy who are trying to get me are driving around and around looking for a place to park, evidently achieving as little as us. The project nearest and dearest to my heart—turning the Bible into rhymed cou­ plets—is coming along fine, with the first one already firmly jelled and on paper— the work of four months, since I had that dream bidding me to take up my pen and do that for the Glory of God, as well as for fun and profit in my spare time. mention_cards.context: Exhausted after writing 110 pages in four days, Dick tells Carol Carr about the new novel, A Scanner Darkly — a somber, tragic book about drug addiction — and explains its title as a pun on Paul's phrase from 1 Corinthians 13. This is the clearest proof that a biblical verse was structural to his fiction before 2-3-74: the title, and with it the novel's governing idea of impaired sight, comes from Paul a year before the visions.
mention_cards.pith: what it is called as a sort of pun on Paul’s phrase, “... We see as through a glass darkly,”
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.context: To his literary agent, five months before 2-3-74, Dick shares a fragment of Ecclesiastes in the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation and says he prefers it to the older version. He then sets three renderings of 1 Corinthians 15:51 side by side — the New World Translation's "Look! I tell you a sacred secret", the King James "Behold I tell you a mystery", and the New English Bible's "Listen! I shall unfold a mystery" — and praises the first as direct and honest. This is close reading of translation, not casual quotation.
mention_cards.pith: The new JW version is so direct, so—honest.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … This is absurd. I’ll never sign such a contract again, but it seems to be NAL’s policy ... .alas.
